To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

## Executive assessment

The Seller’s package is materially seller-favourable. The principal concerns are:

1. **A critical customer consent remains outstanding** for Bluefen, representing approximately 30% of FY26 revenue.
2. **AUD 3.2 million of bank debt and related security would remain at Completion**, contrary to the agreed debt-free/cash-free basis.
3. **AUD 420,000 of Completion bonuses, plus potentially payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs, are omitted from funds flow.**
4. **Ownership of important Ironquay-developed IP is not established.**
5. **The export/privacy incident remains uninvestigated and unquantified.**
6. The proposed liability regime would apply a **20% cap, 18-month deadline and broad exclusions to almost every conceivable Buyer claim**, including title, tax, indemnity and potentially misconduct claims.
7. The Seller seeks to convert the entire data room and public record into disclosure, and to impute broad constructive knowledge to the Buyer.

We should not accept the SPA on this basis.

---

# 1. Liability limitations

## General warranty cap: 20% / AUD 4.8 million

A 20% cap is materially protective of the Seller given the identified unresolved issues and the purchase price of AUD 24 million. It could leave the Buyer bearing most of a loss caused by inaccurate warranties about the business it is acquiring.

### Buyer position

Push for:

- a higher general warranty cap—preferably **50% of the purchase price**, subject to overall deal dynamics;
- **100% of the purchase price** for title, capacity and authority warranties;
- separate liability treatment for tax and specific indemnities;
- no contractual cap for fraud, fraudulent concealment, wilful misconduct or deliberate breach; and
- confirmation that amounts recovered under insurance or from third parties are dealt with through ordinary no-double-recovery provisions, rather than broad exclusions.

## De minimis and basket

The AUD 25,000 de minimis and AUD 250,000 basket are not necessarily unusual in isolation, but the Seller proposes a **deductible basket**, so only losses above AUD 250,000 are recoverable. Together with the low cap and short claim period, this creates an unduly restrictive package.

### Buyer position

Seek:

- a lower de minimis, or aggregation of claims arising from the same or related facts;
- a **tipping basket**, under which all qualifying losses become recoverable once the threshold is exceeded;
- no thresholds for title, capacity, authority, tax, specific indemnities, leakage, debt, transaction expenses, fraud or deliberate breach; and
- express protection against splitting a related series of losses into separate sub-threshold claims.

## Time limits

An 18-month period is short for liabilities that emerge only after a full audit cycle, customer renewal cycle, regulatory investigation or employee claim.

### Buyer position

Seek:

- **24–36 months** for general warranties;
- tax claims until at least the relevant statutory limitation period expires, plus an appropriate buffer;
- title and capacity claims for at least the general statutory limitation period;
- longer periods for employment, privacy/cyber, IP and regulatory matters where exposure may emerge later; and
- specific indemnities surviving until the relevant matter is finally resolved.

A notice should only need to describe the claim in reasonable detail based on information then available. Failure to quantify a claim precisely at notification should not invalidate it.

## Title and fundamental warranties

Applying the general 20% cap and 18-month limit to capacity and title is unacceptable. The Buyer is paying AUD 24 million for 100% ownership. If the Seller cannot convey that interest, the Buyer’s remedy cannot sensibly be limited to AUD 4.8 million.

### Buyer position

Title, capacity, authority, valid issue of shares, absence of encumbrances and ownership of the entire issued capital should:

- be capped at **100% of the purchase price**, plus recoverable enforcement costs;
- have a substantially longer survival period; and
- be excluded from the de minimis and basket.

The share register is relevant evidence but is not conclusive proof of beneficial title, valid issue, absence of encumbrances, options or third-party rights. Require warranties and completion evidence covering those matters.

## Limitations applying to “all Claims”

The proposed wording is exceptionally broad. It may apply the cap, time bar, exclusive-remedy language and non-reliance provisions to:

- specific indemnities;
- debt and purchase-price adjustment obligations;
- post-Completion covenants;
- title and tax claims;
- claims for breach of conditions or Completion obligations;
- restitution, misleading or deceptive conduct and other statutory remedies; and
- fraud or deliberate concealment.

### Buyer position

Define separate claim categories and state expressly that the general warranty limitations do **not** apply to:

- purchase-price adjustments, leakage, debt or transaction-expense obligations;
- specific indemnities;
- tax covenant claims;
- title, capacity and authority claims;
- breaches of pre-Completion and post-Completion covenants;
- fraud, dishonesty, fraudulent concealment, wilful misconduct or deliberate breach;
- equitable relief and specific performance; or
- rights that cannot lawfully be excluded.

Non-reliance and entire-agreement clauses should not excuse inaccurate express warranties or deliberate/misleading disclosures.

---

# 2. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge

## General disclosure of the data room and public records

The Seller seeks to disclose “every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to” in the entire data room, accounts, statutory registers and public records. This improperly transfers the burden to the Buyer to discover inconsistencies, infer legal significance and connect material scattered across multiple documents.

The disclosure cut-off is also **22 September 2026**. Given the current timetable, it may be stale. There is no indication that the Seller has disclosed subsequent developments.

### Buyer position

Require that a matter qualify against a warranty only where it is:

- **fairly and specifically disclosed**;
- disclosed with sufficient detail to identify its nature, scope and reasonably foreseeable consequences;
- cross-referenced to the relevant warranty and source documents; and
- accompanied by complete and accurate underlying documents.

Reject blanket disclosure of:

- the whole data room;
- matters merely “referred to” in documents;
- public registers or matters supposedly discoverable from searches; and
- information disclosed without its material context.

Require:

- a frozen, indexed data-room copy delivered with the executed SPA;
- a final disclosure letter updated to signing and, if signing and Completion are separate, a tightly controlled Completion update;
- no new disclosure after signing without Buyer consent; and
- disclosure not to qualify specific indemnities, covenants or conditions precedent.

Clause 1.4’s “no admission” language is not itself decisive, but it should not dilute whether a matter has been fairly disclosed or the operation of any indemnity.

## Buyer knowledge

The proposed exclusion for anything known by the Buyer **or its advisers**, including anything discoverable in the data room or public records, is too broad. It creates constructive knowledge and could attribute to the Buyer every fact seen by any lawyer, accountant, consultant or technical adviser, regardless of whether it reached the deal decision-makers.

### Buyer position

If a knowledge exclusion is accepted at all:

- limit it to the **actual, conscious knowledge** of a short list of named senior Buyer deal-team members;
- exclude constructive, imputed and deemed knowledge;
- do not attribute adviser knowledge to the Buyer;
- delete “discoverable” or “ought reasonably to have known” standards;
- place the burden of proving knowledge on the Seller; and
- provide that due diligence does not waive rights under express warranties or indemnities.

---

# 3. Bluefen customer consent

Bluefen represents approximately **AUD 3.6 million, or 30%, of FY26 revenue**. No final written consent has been provided, and the Seller has not shown that the conditions in clause 11.3 have been satisfied.

This is not an administrative matter. Loss of or adverse change to this contract could materially affect valuation and the commercial rationale for the acquisition.

### Buyer position

Make Bluefen consent a genuine condition precedent requiring, before Completion:

- final written consent from the correct counterparty;
- satisfaction or waiver, on terms acceptable to the Buyer, of all associated conditions;
- no termination, price reduction, service reduction, accelerated payment, new liability, fee or adverse amendment;
- confirmation that the contract remains in full force; and
- delivery of the complete executed consent and supporting evidence.

The condition should not be deemed satisfied merely because a document labelled “consent” is delivered. The Buyer should approve its form and substance, acting reasonably.

If consent is not obtained by the long-stop date, the Buyer should be able to terminate without liability. Depending on commercial appetite, alternatives could include a price holdback or escrow, but completion without protection against loss of a 30% revenue customer is not recommended.

---

# 4. Riverlark debt and security

The Seller proposes to provide the bank release **after Completion**, even though approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding. That directly conflicts with the debt-free/cash-free deal basis and risks the Buyer acquiring shares in a company whose assets remain subject to security.

### Buyer position

At Completion:

- Riverlark debt must be repaid from the Seller’s Completion proceeds, not funded economically by the Buyer;
- the amount must be included in a formal payoff letter;
- the funds flow must pay Riverlark directly where appropriate;
- executed releases and discharges of all guarantees and security must be delivered;
- PPSR and other security registrations must be discharged, or irrevocable discharge undertakings acceptable to the Buyer must be in place;
- the Company and Buyer group must be fully released from obligations under the facility; and
- any interest, break fee, discharge fee and associated cost must be for the Seller’s account.

A post-Completion promise to obtain a release is not sufficient. Repayment and release should be conditions to Completion or mandatory Completion deliverables, with the Buyer entitled not to complete if they are absent.

---

# 5. Completion bonuses

The AUD 420,000 bonuses arise because of Completion and are omitted from funds flow. The disclosure also does not quantify superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs.

These are transaction-triggered liabilities and should not reduce the value of the Company after Completion.

### Buyer position

Require:

- the bonuses and all related taxes and on-costs to be calculated before Completion;
- payment by the Seller, or a dollar-for-dollar purchase-price reduction/Completion deduction;
- treatment as Seller transaction expenses or leakage, not ordinary working capital;
- confirmation that no additional change-of-control, retention or transaction bonuses exist;
- evidence of payment and satisfaction of associated withholding and superannuation obligations; and
- an indemnity for any omitted or understated amount.

The fact the bonuses are “a matter for the Seller” is helpful only if the documents and funds flow actually ensure the Buyer and Company bear no economic cost.

---

# 6. Ironquay IP

The documents indicate that transfer of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on payment of all SOW3 fees, with AUD 180,000 recorded as open. There is no independent payment evidence or confirmatory assignment.

The Seller’s proposed indemnity, limited to the specific outstanding payment, does not address the real risk: the Company may not own or have sufficient rights to business-critical IP.

### Buyer position

Before Completion require:

- confirmation from Ironquay of all amounts owing;
- payment of all outstanding fees by or for the Seller;
- an executed assignment or acknowledgement confirming that all relevant IP has vested in the Company;
- waiver of liens, retention rights and further claims;
- copies of all SOWs, variations and underlying contractor/employee assignments; and
- verification that the rights include source code, documentation, modifications and the right to use, commercialise and transfer the materials.

The specific indemnity should cover all loss arising from:

- failure of title or insufficient licence rights;
- claims by Ironquay or its personnel;
- infringement or inability to use the materials;
- replacement, redevelopment, migration and remediation costs;
- business interruption and third-party claims; and
- amounts required to perfect ownership.

It should not be confined to AUD 180,000 or merely the payment obligation.

---

# 7. Export/privacy incident

The disclosure indicates that a download link may have exposed approximately 1,240 records to an unintended external email address. The investigation does not establish access, scope or whether notification is required.

It is premature to characterise this as immaterial. Names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps can constitute personal information depending on context, and the event may create privacy, cybersecurity, contractual and reputational exposure.

### Buyer position

Require before Completion:

- a privileged forensic investigation into delivery, access, downloads and onward disclosure;
- identification of the recipient and written confirmation of deletion/non-use;
- preservation of logs and relevant evidence;
- an assessment of obligations under the Privacy Act, Notifiable Data Breaches regime, customer contracts and other applicable requirements;
- copies of communications with the recipient, insurers, affected customers and regulators;
- confirmation that the incident has been contained and remediation completed; and
- disclosure of any similar historical incidents.

Seek a specific indemnity for all pre-Completion incident-related costs and liabilities, including investigation, notification, remediation, customer claims, regulatory action and reasonable professional costs. It should have a separate cap and survival period appropriate to the risk, rather than fall within the AUD 4.8 million/18-month general warranty regime.

Also include an interim covenant requiring prompt notification of further developments and prohibiting regulatory or customer communications without Buyer consultation, to the extent lawful.

---

# 8. Supplier renewals

The three Sandbar renewals total AUD 330,000. The disclosure carefully avoids confirming whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary-course expenditure. The Seller’s assertion that they are ordinary course is not supported by the disclosed facts.

### Buyer position

Obtain:

- the complete contracts, renewal notices and termination provisions;
- renewal dates and service periods;
- confirmation whether commitments were entered into consistently with past practice;
- details of prepayments, accruals, minimum commitments and cancellation fees;
- confirmation whether the costs are captured in working capital, debt-like items or forecasts; and
- evidence that no renewal was accelerated or entered into to benefit the Seller before Completion.

If the costs relate to pre-Completion periods, are overdue, are non-recurring, or were incurred outside ordinary course, they should be accounted for through working capital, debt-like items, leakage or a specific price adjustment. Interim operating covenants should prevent material renewals or commitments without Buyer consent.

---

# 9. Tax and IP warranties

It is not acceptable to place tax and IP entirely within the general 20% cap and 18-month period.

### Tax

Seek:

- a separate tax deed/covenant for pre-Completion tax;
- statutory-period survival plus a buffer;
- no de minimis or basket;
- appropriate control-of-tax-claims provisions; and
- coverage of payroll tax, superannuation, withholding, transaction bonuses and historical tax liabilities.

### IP

Given the Ironquay issue and the nature of an analytics business, require robust warranties concerning:

- ownership and valid licensing of all material IP;
- employee and contractor assignments;
- source code and repositories;
- open-source software compliance;
- infringement claims;
- data rights and permitted use of datasets;
- confidentiality and trade secrets; and
- absence of security interests or restrictions affecting IP.

Known Ironquay exposure should be dealt with through completion steps and a specific indemnity, not merely general warranties.

---

# 10. Other disclosed matters

## Office lease

The disclosure says there is a notification obligation, although apparently no landlord consent requirement. Require the Seller to:

- give the required notice within the contractual period;
- provide evidence of compliance; and
- confirm that the transaction does not trigger termination, rent review, additional security or other adverse consequences.

## Mossvale

The disclosed restriction appears to concern assignment rather than a share sale, but the full contract and any indirect change-of-control language should be checked. Obtain confirmation that the transaction does not trigger termination, default, renegotiation or consent requirements.

## Title

DD-012 should not be the sole protection. Require at Completion:

- original or replacement share certificates;
- executed transfers;
- board resolutions approving registration;
- updated registers;
- releases of any security over the shares;
- confirmation of no options, convertibles, pre-emption rights, trusts or competing beneficial interests; and
- fundamental title warranties backed by appropriate remedies.

---

# Recommended negotiation priorities

## Non-negotiable Completion protections

1. **Bluefen:** final effective consent, with all conditions satisfied and no adverse terms.
2. **Riverlark:** repayment and release of all debt and security at Completion.
3. **Bonuses:** Seller bears the AUD 420,000 plus all on-costs through funds flow or price reduction.
4. **Ironquay:** payment and evidence establishing full IP ownership before Completion.
5. **Incident:** completed investigation, containment evidence and specific indemnity.

## Liability regime

6. Raise the general warranty cap; make title/capacity subject to a 100% cap and longer survival.
7. Establish separate regimes for tax, specific indemnities, covenants and purchase-price obligations.
8. Extend general warranty survival to at least 24–36 months.
9. Prefer a tipping basket and exclude fundamental/specific claims from all thresholds.
10. Carve fraud, deliberate concealment, wilful misconduct and non-excludable statutory rights out of limitations and exclusive-remedy provisions.

## Disclosure and knowledge

11. Reject blanket data-room and public-register disclosure.
12. Require fair, specific, sufficiently detailed disclosure against identified warranties.
13. Limit Buyer knowledge to actual knowledge of named senior individuals, excluding advisers and constructive knowledge.
14. Freeze and index the data room and require an updated disclosure package through signing/Completion.

## Economic mechanics

15. Reconcile all debt, bonuses, transaction expenses, supplier commitments and on-costs in an agreed Completion statement and funds flow.
16. Include no-leakage protection and a dollar-for-dollar remedy for undisclosed debt or Seller transaction expenses.

Overall, the unresolved commercial matters should be fixed through **conditions precedent, Completion deliverables and funds-flow deductions**, rather than left to the general warranty regime. Known risks should be covered by **specific indemnities**, because the Seller’s proposed general limitations would otherwise make recovery difficult and materially incomplete.

- satisfaction or waiver, on terms acceptable to the Buyer, of all associated conditions;
- no termination, price reduction, service reduction, accelerated payment, new liability, fee or adverse amendment;
- confirmation that the contract remains in full force; and
- delivery of the complete executed consent and supporting evidence.

The condition should not be deemed satisfied merely because a document labelled “consent” is delivered. The Buyer should approve its form and substance, acting reasonably.

If consent is not obtained by the long-stop date, the Buyer should be able to terminate without liability. Depending on commercial appetite, alternatives could include a price holdback or escrow, but completion without protection against loss of a 30% revenue customer is not recommended.

---

# 4. Riverlark debt and security

The Seller proposes to provide the bank release **after Completion**, even though approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding. That directly conflicts with the debt-free/cash-free deal basis and risks the Buyer acquiring shares in a company whose assets remain subject to security.

### Buyer position

At Completion:

- Riverlark debt must be repaid from the Seller’s Completion proceeds, not funded economically by the Buyer;
- the amount must be included in a formal payoff letter;
- the funds flow must pay Riverlark directly where appropriate;
- executed releases and discharges of all guarantees and security must be delivered;
- PPSR and other security registrations must be discharged, or irrevocable discharge undertakings acceptable to the Buyer must be in place;
- the Company and Buyer group must be fully released from obligations under the facility; and
- any interest, break fee, discharge fee and associated cost must be for the Seller’s account.

A post-Completion promise to obtain a release is not sufficient. Repayment and release should be conditions to Completion or mandatory Completion deliverables, with the Buyer entitled not to complete if they are absent.

---

# 5. Completion bonuses

The AUD 420,000 bonuses arise because of Completion and are omitted from funds flow. The disclosure also does not quantify superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs.

These are transaction-triggered liabilities and should not reduce the value of the Company after Completion.

### Buyer position

Require:

- the bonuses and all related taxes and on-costs to be calculated before Completion;
- payment by the Seller, or a dollar-for-dollar purchase-price reduction/Completion deduction;
- treatment as Seller transaction expenses or leakage, not ordinary working capital;
- confirmation that no additional change-of-control, retention or transaction bonuses exist;
- evidence of payment and satisfaction of associated withholding and superannuation obligations; and
- an indemnity for any omitted or understated amount.

The fact the bonuses are “a matter for the Seller” is helpful only if the documents and funds flow actually ensure the Buyer and Company bear no economic cost.

---

# 6. Ironquay IP

The documents indicate that transfer of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on payment of all SOW3 fees, with AUD 180,000 recorded as open. There is no independent payment evidence or confirmatory assignment.

The Seller’s proposed indemnity, limited to the specific outstanding payment, does not address the real risk: the Company may not own or have sufficient rights to business-critical IP.

### Buyer position

Before Completion require:

- confirmation from Ironquay of all amounts owing;
- payment of all outstanding fees by or for the Seller;
- an executed assignment or acknowledgement confirming that all relevant IP has vested in the Company;
- waiver of liens, retention rights and further claims;
- copies of all SOWs, variations and underlying contractor/employee assignments; and
- verification that the rights include source code, documentation, modifications and the right to use, commercialise and transfer the materials.

The specific indemnity should cover all loss arising from:

- failure of title or insufficient licence rights;
- claims by Ironquay or its personnel;
- infringement or inability to use the materials;
- replacement, redevelopment, migration and remediation costs;
- business interruption and third-party claims; and
- amounts required to perfect ownership.

It should not be confined to AUD 180,000 or merely the payment obligation.

# 7. Export/privacy incident

The disclosure indicates that a download link may have exposed approximately 1,240 records to an unintended external email address. The investigation does not establish access, scope or whether notification is required.

It is premature to characterise this as immaterial. Names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps can constitute personal information depending on context, and the event may create privacy, cybersecurity, contractual and reputational exposure.

### Buyer position

Require before Completion:

- a privileged forensic investigation into delivery, access, downloads and onward disclosure;
- identification of the recipient and written confirmation of deletion/non-use;
- preservation of logs and relevant evidence;
- an assessment of obligations under the Privacy Act, Notifiable Data Breaches regime, customer contracts and other applicable requirements;
- copies of communications with the recipient, insurers, affected customers and regulators;
- confirmation that the incident has been contained and remediation completed; and
- disclosure of any similar historical incidents.

Seek a specific indemnity for all pre-Completion incident-related costs and liabilities, including investigation, notification, remediation, customer claims, regulatory action and reasonable professional costs. It should have a separate cap and survival period appropriate to the risk, rather than fall within the AUD 4.8 million/18-month general warranty regime.

Also include an interim covenant requiring prompt notification of further developments and prohibiting regulatory or customer communications without Buyer consultation, to the extent lawful.

# 8. Supplier renewals

The three Sandbar renewals total AUD 330,000. The disclosure carefully avoids confirming whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary-course expenditure. The Seller’s assertion that they are ordinary course is not supported by the disclosed facts.

### Buyer position

Obtain:

- the complete contracts, renewal notices and termination provisions;
- renewal dates and service periods;
- confirmation whether commitments were entered into consistently with past practice;
- details of prepayments, accruals, minimum commitments and cancellation fees;
- confirmation whether the costs are captured in working capital, debt-like items or forecasts; and
- evidence that no renewal was accelerated or entered into to benefit the Seller before Completion.

If the costs relate to pre-Completion periods, are overdue, are non-recurring, or were incurred outside ordinary course, they should be accounted for through working capital, debt-like items, leakage or a specific price adjustment. Interim operating covenants should prevent material renewals or commitments without Buyer consent.

# 9. Tax and IP warranties

It is not acceptable to place tax and IP entirely within the general 20% cap and 18-month period.

### Tax

Seek:

- a separate tax deed/covenant for pre-Completion tax;
- statutory-period survival plus a buffer;
- no de minimis or basket;
- appropriate control-of-tax-claims provisions; and
- coverage of payroll tax, superannuation, withholding, transaction bonuses and historical tax liabilities.

### IP

Given the Ironquay issue and the nature of an analytics business, require robust warranties concerning:

- ownership and valid licensing of all material IP;
- employee and contractor assignments;
- source code and repositories;
- open-source software compliance;
- infringement claims;
- data rights and permitted use of datasets;
- confidentiality and trade secrets; and
- absence of security interests or restrictions affecting IP.

Known Ironquay exposure should be dealt with through completion steps and a specific indemnity, not merely general warranties.

# 10. Other disclosed matters

## Office lease

The disclosure says there is a notification obligation, although apparently no landlord consent requirement. Require the Seller to:

- give the required notice within the contractual period;
- provide evidence of compliance; and
- confirm that the transaction does not trigger termination, rent review, additional security or other adverse consequences.

## Mossvale

The disclosed restriction appears to concern assignment rather than a share sale, but the full contract and any indirect change-of-control language should be checked. Obtain confirmation that the transaction does not trigger termination, default, renegotiation or consent requirements.

## Title

DD-012 should not be the sole protection. Require at Completion:

- original or replacement share certificates;
- executed transfers;
- board resolutions approving registration;
- updated registers;
- releases of any security over the shares;
- confirmation of no options, convertibles, pre-emption rights, trusts or competing beneficial interests; and
- fundamental title warranties backed by appropriate remedies.

# Recommended negotiation priorities

## Non-negotiable Completion protections

1. **Bluefen:** final effective consent, with all conditions satisfied and no adverse terms.
2. **Riverlark:** repayment and release of all debt and security at Completion.
3. **Bonuses:** Seller bears the AUD 420,000 plus all on-costs through funds flow or price reduction.
4. **Ironquay:** payment and evidence establishing full IP ownership before Completion.
5. **Incident:** completed investigation, containment evidence and specific indemnity.

## Liability regime

6. Raise the general warranty cap; make title/capacity subject to a 100% cap and longer survival.
7. Establish separate regimes for tax, specific indemnities, covenants and purchase-price obligations.
8. Extend general warranty survival to at least 24–36 months.
9. Prefer a tipping basket and exclude fundamental/specific claims from all thresholds.
10. Carve fraud, deliberate concealment, wilful misconduct and non-excludable statutory rights out of limitations and exclusive-remedy provisions.

## Disclosure and knowledge

11. Reject blanket data-room and public-register disclosure.
12. Require fair, specific, sufficiently detailed disclosure against identified warranties.
13. Limit Buyer knowledge to actual knowledge of named senior individuals, excluding advisers and constructive knowledge.
14. Freeze and index the data room and require an updated disclosure package through signing/Completion.

## Economic mechanics

15. Reconcile all debt, bonuses, transaction expenses, supplier commitments and on-costs in an agreed Completion statement and funds flow.
16. Include no-leakage protection and a dollar-for-dollar remedy for undisclosed debt or Seller transaction expenses.

Overall, the unresolved commercial matters should be fixed through **conditions precedent, Completion deliverables and funds-flow deductions**, rather than left to the general warranty regime. Known risks should be covered by **specific indemnities**, because the Seller’s proposed general limitations would otherwise make recovery difficult and materially incomplete.
